claims: The Tax Court has found that an Arabian horse breeding and showing operation can be classified as a hobby rather than a business if the activity is not engaged in for profit
In Marcia Trescott Helmick & Robert P. Helmick v. Commissioner, the court noted that the disallowance of losses under section 183 applies unless the activity is entered into for profit
The Tax Court considers factors such as the taxpayer's intent and the manner in which the activity is conducted to determine if the primary objective is profit

verdicts.why: Sources state section 183 disallows losses for activities not entered into for profit, including hobbies.
T.C. Memo. 2009-220 explicitly states section 183 disallows losses unless activity entered into for profit.
Sources confirm Tax Court considers intent, manner of activity, expertise, time/effort, and personal motives.

claims: For the tax year 2026, a social media influencer cannot deduct cable and streaming subscriptions as business expenses
The Tax Court has held that cable and streaming subscription expenses are considered personal unless they are directly related to the business
In the case of Mr. Sami, the court found that television and video streaming expenses were not directly related to business activities
In the case of Mr. Sami, the court found that television and video streaming expenses were primarily for personal enjoyment
Television and video streaming expenses that are personal and not directly related to business are not deductible under section 162(a)

verdicts.why: Sources address Mr. Sami's 2019-2021 expenses, not tax year 2026 hypotheticals.
T.C. Memo 2026-69 cites Minick v. Commissioner stating television and cable bills are not deductible unless directly related to business.
T.C. Memo 2026-69 explicitly found Mr. Sami's television and video streaming expenses were not directly related to his business activities.
T.C. Memo 2026-69 states viewing television is a common source of personal enjoyment and was not convinced expenses were directly related to business.
Sources establish personal entertainment expenses are not deductible under section 162(a) unless primarily for business purposes.

claims: The Tax Court has treated farm workers who were provided housing, insurance, and pay advances by the farm as employees for purposes of Federal employment taxes
Farm workers who maintained their primary residence on the farm in a trailer provided by the employer and had an ongoing rather than transitory or temporary relationship were found to be employees
When an employer covers job-related expenses and provides workers' compensation and employer's liability insurance, this supports the existence of an employment relationship
When a farm worker received an advance on their weekly compensation, their subsequent checks were reduced to repay the advanced amount

verdicts.why: T.C. Memo. 2012-184 holds workers were employees, noting petitioner purchased workers' compensation and employer's liability insurance.
T.C. Memo. 2012-184 at *11-13 explicitly states workers' residence on farm and ongoing relationship supported employer-employee classification.
T.C. Memo. 2012-184 at *11-13 states these factors are indicative of intention to create employment relationship.
T.C. Memo. 2012-184 at *4-6 describes advance repayment procedure where subsequent checks were reduced.

claims: Toll and parking charges on a spreadsheet are not sufficient to substantiate travel expenses
Each element of a traveling expense must be substantiated through adequate records or sufficient evidence corroborating the taxpayer's own statement
The taxpayer must provide detailed records that clearly correspond with travel destinations and corroborate their assertions
A spreadsheet lacking specificity and detail fails to substantiate claimed travel expenses

verdicts.why: T.C. Memo. 2023-4 shows toll and parking charges on spreadsheet failed substantiation; expenses didn't clearly correspond with travel logs.
Section 274(d) explicitly requires adequate records or sufficient evidence corroborating taxpayer's own statement for traveling expenses.
T.C. Memo. 2023-4 held disputed expenses didn't clearly correspond with travel logs and lacked required specificity and detail.
T.C. Memo. 2023-4 held spreadsheet lacking specificity and detail failed to satisfy section 274 substantiation requirements.

claims: For the tax year 2026, a taxpayer must recognize income upon the termination of a life insurance policy if the policy's cash surrender value is used to satisfy outstanding loans against the policy
Using a life insurance policy's cash surrender value to satisfy outstanding loans against the policy is treated as a constructive distribution of income
The Tax Court has held that using a policy's cash surrender value to satisfy outstanding loans constitutes a taxable event
An indirect distribution of an insurance policy's cash surrender value is recognized as gross income under section 72

verdicts.why: T.C. Memo. 2026-33 discusses 2015 tax year, not 2026 tax year.
T.C. Memo. 2026-33 at *8 states loan repayment is treated as if cash value transferred and taxpayer repaid loans.
T.C. Memo. 2026-33 at *8 holds Sawyer received taxable constructive distribution when policy terminated.
T.C. Memo. 2026-33 at *7-8 explicitly states indirect distribution of insurance policy cash surrender value is recognized as gross income under section 72.

claims: For tax year 2026, rental owners with modified adjusted gross income over $100,000 may receive a portion of the $25,000 rental loss allowance
The $25,000 rental loss allowance is reduced by 50% of the amount by which modified adjusted gross income exceeds $100,000
The $25,000 rental loss allowance is completely phased out at modified adjusted gross income of $150,000 or more
If modified adjusted gross income is between $100,000 and $150,000, the rental loss allowance is limited by the phase-out

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 469(i)(3)(A) states the $25,000 amount is reduced by 50% of AGI exceeding $100,000, allowing partial allowance.
26 U.S.C. § 469(i)(3)(A) explicitly states the reduction is 50% of the amount by which AGI exceeds $100,000.
IRS Pub 527 states 'if your MAGI is $150,000 or more, there is no special allowance' and 26 U.S.C. § 469(i)(3)(A) confirms.
The phase-out mechanism in 26 U.S.C. § 469(i)(3)(A) applies between $100,000 and $150,000 MAGI, reducing the allowance.

claims: To determine whether an Arabian horse breeding activity is a business or a hobby, the primary objective of the activity must be to make a profit, assessed by considering all facts and circumstances including the taxpayer's intent and the manner in which the activity is conducted
A taxpayer's expertise, research, and consultation with experts can indicate a profit objective
The Tax Court looks for evidence that a taxpayer sought professional advice on running the business profitably, rather than just general advice typical of a hobbyist
The amount of time and effort devoted to an activity is a significant factor in determining business versus hobby status
If a taxpayer engages in an activity as a full-time endeavor, this supports a profit motive
The way an activity is conducted, including whether it is carried out in a businesslike manner, can indicate a profit objective
Maintaining proper records and having a business plan are relevant to whether an activity is conducted in a businesslike manner
Personal enjoyment in an activity may suggest a hobby but does not automatically classify the activity as such if there is evidence of a profit motive
The Tax Court emphasizes the need for a predominant profit motive in determining business versus hobby status

verdicts.why: Sources establish profit objective as primary test using all facts and circumstances including intent and manner of conducting activity.
Treas. Reg. § 1.183-2(b)(2) states taxpayer expertise, research, and expert consultation may indicate profit objective.
Sources distinguish professional consultant advice on profitable business operations from general hobbyist advice, citing Betts precedent.
Treas. Reg. § 1.183-2(b)(3) identifies time and effort devoted to activity as significant factor in determining business status.
Sources do not state that full-time engagement automatically supports profit motive; no such categorical rule appears.
Sources repeatedly cite manner of conducting activity as factor indicating business-like operation and profit objective.
Sources do not mention maintaining records or business plans as relevant to businesslike manner determination.
Sources state personal pleasure may indicate no-profit activity but does not automatically classify as hobby if profit evidence exists.
Ninth Circuit precedent Wolf requires predominant, primary, or principal profit objective for deduction allowance.

claims: A client who fully owns and manages rental houses counts as actively participating in the rental real estate activity
Active participation requires owning at least 10% of the rental property
Active participation requires making management decisions in a significant and bona fide sense, such as approving tenants and deciding on rental terms
The Tax Court in Mohamad Nasser Aboui & Mahyar Mizani v. Commissioner allowed taxpayers to deduct losses as active participants in rental real estate
Ownership and management of rental properties can establish active participation for the rental loss allowance

verdicts.why: IRS Pub 527 states material participation requires involvement in operations on regular, continuous, substantial basis; managing rental houses constitutes such involvement.
26 U.S.C. § 469(i)(6)(A) states interest must be at least 10% by value for active participation treatment.
Sources define active participation but do not specify management decisions like approving tenants or deciding rental terms.
T.C. Memo. 2024-106 held taxpayers may deduct $25,000 in real estate losses as active participants in rental activities.
Multiple sources indicate ownership and management of rental properties can establish active participation for the $25,000 loss allowance.

claims: A farm can challenge the IRS's reclassification of its contract workers as employees in Tax Court
An employer may petition Tax Court for review of employee classification and the proper amount of employment tax owed as a result of that classification
The Tax Court has found that providing housing to workers is indicative of an employer-employee relationship rather than an independent contractor relationship
The Tax Court has found that covering job-related expenses is indicative of an employer-employee relationship rather than an independent contractor relationship
In a Tax Court case, the long-term nature of workers' residence on a farm supported the conclusion that the workers were employees for federal employment tax purposes
In a Tax Court case, the provision of advances on workers' compensation supported the conclusion that the workers were employees for federal employment tax purposes

verdicts.why: T.C. Memo. 2012-184 shows farm filed petition in Tax Court challenging IRS worker classification determination under section 7436.
T.C. Memo. 2009-234 states employer may petition Tax Court for review of employee classification and employment tax amount under sections 7436(a) and (b).
T.C. Memo. 2012-184 at *11-13 states providing residence on property supports employer-employee relationship, not independent contractor.
T.C. Memo. 2012-184 at *11-13 states covering job-related expenses is indicative of employment relationship rather than independent contractor.
T.C. Memo. 2012-184 at *11-13 finds long-term residence on farm supports employer-employee relationship for tax purposes.
T.C. Memo. 2012-184 at *4-6 shows workers received advances on weekly compensation; at *11-13 discusses relationship factors supporting employment.

claims: For tax year 2026, taxpayers must maintain adequate and detailed records to substantiate travel expenses, including a daily diary or record of expenditures that identifies the amount and nature of each expenditure
For tax year 2026, taxpayers must maintain supporting documents for larger travel expenses
The burden of proof is on the taxpayer to show that travel expenses are ordinary and necessary business expenses
The Tax Court has held that a spreadsheet lacking specificity and detail does not satisfy the substantiation requirements for travel expenses
Travel expenses must clearly correspond with travel destinations and be corroborated by testimony or supporting documentation

verdicts.why: 26 CFR 1.162-17(d)(2) states taxpayers should maintain 'adequate and detailed records' including 'daily diary or record of expenditures' with sufficient detail to identify amount and nature.
26 CFR 1.162-17(d)(2) requires 'supporting documents, especially in connection with large or exceptional expenditures.'
26 CFR 1.162-17(d)(2) explicitly states 'burden of proof is upon the taxpayer to show that such expenses...constitute ordinary and necessary business expenses.'
T.C. Memo. 2023-4 states disputed spreadsheet 'lacks the specificity and detail required' under section 274 substantiation requirements.
T.C. Memo. 2023-4 holds expenses 'do not clearly correspond with the travel destinations on petitioners' travel logs' and lacks corroborating testimony.

claims: For tax year 2026, income is constructively received when it is credited to a taxpayer's account, set apart for them, or otherwise made available so that they may draw upon it at any time
For tax year 2026, income is constructively received when a taxpayer could have drawn upon it during the taxable year if notice of intention to withdraw had been given
Income is not constructively received if the taxpayer's control over its receipt is subject to substantial limitations or restrictions
In Jonathan D. Sawyer v. Commissioner, the Tax Court held that Mr. Sawyer constructively received taxable income from the termination of his life insurance policy
In Jonathan D. Sawyer v. Commissioner, the cash surrender value of Mr. Sawyer's life insurance policy was used to satisfy outstanding loans against the policy, resulting in a deemed distribution

verdicts.why: 26 CFR 1.451-2(a) states income is constructively received when credited to account, set apart, or made available to draw upon at any time.
26 CFR 1.451-2(a) includes income constructively received if could have been drawn upon during year if notice of withdrawal given.
26 CFR 1.451-2(a) states income not constructively received if control subject to substantial limitations or restrictions.
T.C. Memo. 2026-33 holds Mr. Sawyer constructively received taxable income from policy termination at page 12-13.
T.C. Memo. 2026-33 at page 8 states cash surrender value applied against outstanding loans creating deemed distribution.

claims: Under the Internal Revenue Code, personal expenses are generally not deductible
Section 262 states that no deduction is allowed for personal, living, or family expenses
Expenses for television and video streaming are considered personal expenses unless they are primarily incurred for business purposes
An influencer cannot deduct streaming subscriptions as business expenses if they are primarily for personal use

verdicts.why: Sources discuss personal expenses not being deductible but do not state this as a general rule under the Internal Revenue Code.
Section 262 is not cited or discussed in the provided sources.
Sources state television/video streaming expenses are personal unless primarily for business purposes, citing Minick v. Commissioner.
T.C. Memo. 2026-69 holds that streaming subscriptions are not deductible if personal use motivation exists, not just business-related.

claims: For tax year 2026, a taxpayer can exclude gain from the sale of a principal residence if the taxpayer owned and used the property as a principal residence for at least 2 years during the 5-year period ending on the date of sale
The client owned and lived in her house for 3 of the last 5 years
The client meets the ownership and use tests required for the section 121 exclusion
The section 121 exclusion is limited to $250,000 for single taxpayers
The client's gain is $200,000
The client can exclude the entire gain from her taxable income

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 121(a) states gain exclusion requires owned and used as principal residence for 2+ years during 5-year period ending on sale date.
No source provides information about the client's specific ownership and use history.
No source provides facts about whether the client meets the specific ownership and use tests.
Sources do not state the dollar limitation amount for section 121 exclusion.
No source provides information about the client's gain amount.
Cannot determine exclusion eligibility without facts about client's ownership, use, and whether nonqualified use applies.

claims: For the tax year 2026, the maximum deduction for student loan interest is $2,500
The student loan interest deduction is subject to a limitation based on modified adjusted gross income (MAGI)
The student loan interest deduction is reduced if the taxpayer's MAGI exceeds $50,000 for single filers
The student loan interest deduction is reduced if the taxpayer's MAGI exceeds $100,000 for joint returns
The reduction in the student loan interest deduction is calculated based on the excess over the MAGI thresholds

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 221(b)(1) states maximum deduction shall not exceed $2,500.
26 U.S.C. § 221(b)(2) explicitly provides limitation based on modified adjusted gross income.
26 U.S.C. § 221(b)(2)(B)(i)(II) specifies $50,000 threshold for single filers.
26 U.S.C. § 221(b)(2)(B)(i)(II) specifies $100,000 threshold for joint returns.
26 U.S.C. § 221(b)(2)(B) describes reduction calculation based on excess over thresholds.

claims: For tax year 2026, unreimbursed medical expenses are deductible only to the extent they exceed 7.5% of AGI
When unreimbursed medical expenses total $9,000 and the AGI threshold is $7,500, the deductible amount is $1,500

verdicts.why: Sources do not address 2026 tax year or current medical expense deduction threshold rules.
Arithmetic is correct: 7.5% × $100,000 = $7,500.
If threshold is $7,500 and expenses are $9,000, then $9,000 - $7,500 = $1,500 deductible.

claims: For tax year 2026, the $8,000 spent investigating a business before it opened cannot be deducted as a start-up expenditure
Under section 195 of the Internal Revenue Code, no deduction is allowed for start-up expenditures except as provided in that section
If a taxpayer elects to deduct start-up expenditures, they can deduct the lesser of $5,000 or the amount of start-up expenditures up to $50,000 in the year the active trade or business begins
Remainder start-up expenditures are amortized over 180 months
Since the total start-up expenditures exceed $50,000, the deduction is reduced and the client cannot deduct the full $8,000 in the first year

verdicts.why: Sources state start-up expenditures can be deducted if election made; claim says cannot be deducted.
26 U.S.C. § 195(a) states no deduction allowed except as provided in section.
Section 195(b)(1)(A)(ii) limits deduction to $5,000 reduced by excess over $50,000, not up to $50,000.
26 U.S.C. § 195(b)(1)(B) provides remainder deducted ratably over 180-month period.
Claim assumes $8,000 exceeds $50,000 threshold; it does not, so full $8,000 deductible in year one.

claims: For the tax year 2026, a taxpayer can deduct a net capital loss against ordinary income up to $3,000
Any remaining net capital loss is carried over to future years
A taxpayer with a $10,000 net capital loss can deduct $3,000 in the current year
A taxpayer with a $10,000 net capital loss can carry over $7,000 to subsequent years

verdicts.why: Sources do not address the $3,000 capital loss deduction limit for individuals in 2026 or any year.
Sources address corporate capital loss carryovers, not individual net capital loss carryovers.
Sources do not specify the $3,000 annual deduction limit for individual capital losses.
Sources do not address individual capital loss carryover mechanics or amounts.

claims: For tax year 2026, if a taxpayer receives any amount from a qualified retirement plan such as a 401(k), the taxpayer's tax for that year is increased by an amount equal to 10 percent of the portion of the amount that is includible in gross income
A taxpayer who is under age 59½ is subject to the 10-percent additional tax on distributions from qualified retirement plans
A 45-year-old who withdrew $20,000 from a qualified retirement plan is subject to the 10-percent additional tax on that $20,000

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 72(t)(1) states tax is increased by 10% of portion includible in gross income for any qualified retirement plan distribution, with no year limitation.
§ 72(t)(1) imposes 10% tax on distributions but § 72(v)(2) shows exceptions exist; no age-based exemption stated for § 72(t)(1) distributions in provided sources.
Sources establish 10% additional tax applies to qualified retirement plan distributions but do not confirm age 45 qualifies for or is exempt from this tax.

claims: For tax year 2026, the maximum exclusion from gross income for educational assistance provided by an employer is $5,250
If educational assistance exceeds $5,250, only the first $5,250 is excluded from gross income

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 127(a)(2) establishes a $5,250 maximum exclusion for educational assistance per calendar year.
26 U.S.C. § 127(a)(2) states section applies only to first $5,250 when assistance exceeds that amount.

claims: For tax year 2026, no deduction is allowed for any charitable contribution of $250 or more unless the taxpayer substantiates the contribution by a contemporaneous written acknowledgment from the donee organization
The acknowledgment must include the amount of cash contributed
The acknowledgment must include a description of any property contributed
The acknowledgment must state whether the donee provided any goods or services in consideration for the contribution
The acknowledgment must include a good faith estimate of the value of any goods or services provided, or a statement if they consist solely of intangible religious benefits

The acknowledgment is considered contemporaneous if obtained on or before the earlier of the date the taxpayer files a return for the taxable year or the due date for filing such return, including extensions

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 170(f)(8)(A) states no deduction allowed for contributions of $250 or more without contemporaneous written acknowledgment.
26 U.S.C. § 170(f)(8)(B)(i) requires acknowledgment to include the amount of cash contributed.

26 U.S.C. § 170(f)(8)(B)(iii) requires good faith estimate of value or statement regarding intangible religious benefits.
26 U.S.C. § 170(f)(8)(C) defines contemporaneous as on or before earlier of filing date or due date including extensions.

claims: For tax year 2026, like-kind exchange treatment under Section 1031 applies only to exchanges of real property held for use in a trade or business or for investment
For tax year 2026, like-kind exchange treatment under Section 1031 does not apply to exchanges of personal property
For tax year 2026, like-kind exchange treatment under Section 1031 does not apply to exchanges of business equipment

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 1031(a)(1) states like-kind exchange applies only to real property held for productive use in trade or business or investment.
26 U.S.C. § 1031(a)(1) limits like-kind exchanges to real property only, excluding personal property.
Business equipment is personal property, not real property; Section 1031(a) applies only to real property.
Section 1031 applies only to real property; business equipment is personal property and thus excluded.

claims: An employer values an employee's personal use of a company car under the cents-per-mile rule by multiplying the total number of personal miles driven by the employee by the standard mileage rate provided in the applicable Revenue Ruling or Revenue Procedure
The cents-per-mile rule applies if the vehicle is expected to be regularly used in the employer's trade or business or meets certain mileage requirements
The cents-per-mile rate covers the fair market value of maintenance and insurance for the vehicle

If fuel is not provided by the employer, the cents-per-mile rate may be reduced by no more than 5.5 cents

26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(3)(iii) states fair market value of services not specifically identified not reflected in rate.
